captions: Welcome to Camday.
This lesson was written by the Camday teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 8: Forces and Motion.
Kicking a football, swinging a cricket bat, a rocket taking off,
a car braking at the lights: every action involves forces.
Transport produces about one-fifth of the world's carbon dioxide emissions.
Understanding forces and motion can help us design more fuel-efficient vehicles.
Speed tells us how fast something is moving:
the distance travelled in each unit of time.
People walk at about 1 metre per second, run at about 3,
a car might go 15, a train 30,
and a plane about 250 metres per second!
An object that isn't moving has zero speed.
To calculate speed, divide the distance travelled by the time taken.
The SI unit is metres per second.
For longer journeys, we often use kilometres per hour.
Let's try it. An Olympic athlete runs 100 metres in 10 seconds.
Speed equals 100 metres divided by 10 seconds: 10 metres per second.
Speed matters everywhere in daily life.
Here are four places where people measure it.
Walking to school, most people move at about 1.4 metres every second,
so one kilometre takes about twelve minutes.
Near schools, speed limits are lower.
A slower car travels less distance while the driver reacts,
so it can stop in time.
On sports day, a 100 metre race can be timed electronically.
Speed is the distance divided by the time on the clock.
Airline pilots work out how long a flight takes by
dividing the distance by the average speed of the plane.
In every example, speed is the distance travelled divided by the time taken.
Pause and think of one more place where speed matters.
We can rearrange the speed equation using a speed triangle.
Cover the quantity you want to find.
Distance equals speed times time, and time equals distance divided by speed.
A car travels 150 kilometres at 50 kilometres per hour.
How long is the journey?
Cover t: time equals 150 divided by 50, which is 3 hours.
Units really matter. In 1999,
NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter crashed because one team calculated thrust in imperial units,
and another in metric units.
The spacecraft flew too close to Mars and was destroyed.
An athlete doesn't run at the same speed all race.
At the start, she accelerates: she covers more distance each second, 5 metres,
then 6, then 7, then 8.
At the end, she decelerates: she covers less distance each second before stopping.
So we use average speed: total distance divided by total time.
In the first three seconds, she runs 5 plus 6 plus 7,
which is 18 metres.
18 metres divided by 3 seconds gives an average speed of 6 metres per second.
How do police know if a driver is speeding?
A radar speed camera sends out radio waves,
which bounce off a moving vehicle.
The camera uses the returning waves to work out the vehicle's speed.
A two-point camera system photographs a vehicle at two
places a known distance apart and records the times.
Then it calculates the average speed between them.
In the lab, we can use timing gates.
A card on a toy car breaks an infrared beam,
which starts and stops a timer very accurately.
Races are timed electronically to a thousandth of a second,
much more accurately than a stopwatch, which depends on human reaction time.
chapters: Real life: speed all around us

captions: A distance–time graph shows how an object moves.
Time goes along the horizontal axis, and distance up the vertical axis.
A flat, horizontal line means the object isn't moving:
its distance stays the same.
A straight line sloping upwards means a constant speed:
the same distance is covered every second.
A curved line means the speed is changing.
If it gets steeper, the object is speeding up.
The steeper the line, the faster the object is moving.
Let's plot Lee's run.
First, he runs 8 kilometres in 1 hour at a constant speed:
a straight line sloping upwards, from A to B.
Then he rests for half an hour.
His distance doesn't change, so the line from B to C is horizontal.
Finally, he runs another 8 kilometres, taking 1.5 hours.
The line from C to D slopes upwards again,
but it's less steep than A to B, because he's running more slowly.
Graphs help us compare.
A cheetah and a man start running from the same place.
The cheetah's line is very steep at first: it's much faster.
But after about 20 seconds, its line goes flat.
The cheetah has stopped, after 400 metres.
The man's line is less steep, but it keeps rising steadily.
He can't match the cheetah's speed, but he keeps going.
Where the two lines cross, the man overtakes the cheetah,
and he carries on to 800 metres.
Fast isn't everything: endurance matters too!
A cyclist rides to school.
Her distance from home is recorded every 20 seconds.
For the first 40 seconds the line is straight and steep:
she covers 100 metres every 20 seconds.
From 40 to 60 seconds the line is flat while she waits at traffic lights.
Then she rides on, but the line is less steep.
Pause and decide: what was her speed in the first 40 seconds,
and was she faster or slower after the traffic lights?
chapters: Real data: a cyclist's journey to school

captions: Forces have both size and direction, so we draw them as arrows.
In a tug of war,
if both sides pull with 5 newtons in opposite directions,
the forces are balanced.
Counting one direction as positive, the resultant force is 5 minus 5,
which is zero, and the rope doesn't move.
Balanced forces don't change an object's motion.
A lorry at constant speed has its engine force balanced by friction.
And when a skydiver's air resistance equals the pull of gravity,
he falls at a steady speed called the terminal speed.
Two paper cones have the same mass,
but one is much wider than the other.
They are dropped together from the same height.
Predict: which will land first?
Pause and decide.
Watch. Both cones start to fall, and air pushes up against each one.
The small cone lands first.
The large cone falls slowly and lands later.
Explain what you saw.
Both cones have the same weight pulling them down.
The large cone has a bigger surface area,
so there is more air resistance pushing up on it.
The forces on it become balanced at a lower speed,
so it falls more slowly.
Parachutes use the same idea.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
If the forces don't cancel out, they're unbalanced, and the motion changes.
Push a ball right with 12 newtons and left with 5 newtons:
the resultant force is 12 minus 5,
which is 7 newtons to the right.
The ball accelerates to the right.
Here's a worked example.
A box has 100 newtons and 50 newtons pushing right,
and 180 newtons pushing left.
Counting right as positive: 100 plus 50 minus 180 is minus 30.
So the resultant force is 30 newtons to the left,
and the box moves left.
Unbalanced forces can speed things up, like a car accelerating; slow them down,
like friction stopping a sliding book; or change their direction,
like a bat hitting a ball.
Air resistance grows with speed and surface area,
so streamlined shapes and lower speeds help vehicles use less fuel.
chapters: Predict, watch, explain: falling paper cones

captions: Opening a jar, pressing a light switch, cutting with scissors, lifting a wheelbarrow:
each uses the turning effect of a force, called a moment.
A moment makes an object rotate around a pivot point, called the fulcrum.
A door turns about its hinges.
Push near the edge, far from the hinges, and it opens easily.
Push near the hinges, and it's very hard!
The moment depends on the size of the force and its distance from the fulcrum:
moment equals force times distance, M equals F times d,
measured in newton metres.
A motorist pushes on a wheel wrench with 70 newtons,
0.4 metres from the nut.
The moment is 70 times 0.4, which is 28 newton metres.
That's why a long spanner makes nuts easier to loosen.
Like forces, moments have direction.
On a seesaw, the girl's weight turns it one way, anticlockwise,
and the boy's weight turns it the other way, clockwise.
A seesaw is a lever: a simple machine that turns around a fulcrum.
Scissors, wheelbarrows, staplers and pliers are levers too.
So are the bones and joints in our bodies.
Galileo found that a lever's balance depends on both
the weights and their distances from the pivot.
A ruler balances on a pivot at its centre.
Two coins sit 10 centimetres to the left of the pivot.
Predict: where must one coin go on the right to balance the ruler?
Pause and decide.
Watch. One coin placed 10 centimetres to the right is not enough.
The ruler tips to the left.
Moved to 20 centimetres from the pivot,
the single coin balances the two coins.
Explain what you saw.
Two coins at 10 centimetres give the same
turning effect as one coin at 20 centimetres,
because force times distance is equal: 2 times 10 equals 1 times 20.
When the anticlockwise moment equals the clockwise moment, the ruler balances.
This is the principle of moments.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Now it is your turn to shine!

Question 1: A cyclist rides 600 m in 120 s.
What is her average speed?
Pause the video now.
Answer: 5 m/s.
Question 2: What does a horizontal line on a distance–time graph show?
Pause the video now.
Answer: The object is not moving.
Question 3: Forces of 20 N right and 8 N left act on a trolley.
What is the resultant force?
Pause the video now.
Answer: 12 N to the right.
Question 4: A force of 50 N acts 0.2 m from a pivot.
What is the moment?
Pause the video now.
Answer: 10 Nm.
